lines.text: Ancient kingdoms, a homegrown alphabet, colonial rule and a war that split a nation. This is the story of South Korea, from legend to K-pop.
Tradition says the first Korean kingdom, Gojoseon, was founded by Dangun over four thousand years ago. It fell to Han China in 108 BCE.
Then came the Three Kingdoms. Silla, in the south-east, would unite most of the peninsula in 668, and fill it with Buddhist art and learning.
On the Han River, a capital of the rival kingdom Baekje grew up. Centuries later it would become Seoul, the heart of the nation.
In 918 the kingdom of Goryeo arose, and gave Korea its name. Its craftsmen made fine celadon and printed books with movable metal type.
Goryeo's monks carved the Buddhist scriptures onto more than eighty thousand wooden blocks. The Tripitaka Koreana is still kept at Haeinsa temple.
In 1392 the Joseon dynasty began. It would rule from Seoul for more than five centuries, built on Neo-Confucian ideals.
Its kings lived in Gyeongbokgung, the great palace of Seoul, burned in the Japanese invasions and rebuilt centuries later.
Joseon's most beloved ruler was Sejong the Great, whose court pushed forward science, farming and printing.
His greatest gift was Hangul, an alphabet made to be easy to learn, so ordinary people could read and write their own language.
In the 1590s Japan invaded. Admiral Yi Sun-sin beat back its fleets again and again with his armoured turtle ships, and died in his last battle.
Syngman Rhee, a fighter for independence, would one day become the South's first president, until students drove him out in 1960.
In 1910 Japan annexed Korea. Thirty-five years of colonial rule began.
Park Chung Hee, a future general, would seize power in 1961 and drive the country's fast growth with an iron hand.
On the first of March 1919, Koreans read out a declaration of independence and protested across the land. Japan crushed it, but the movement lived on.
Kim Dae-jung would survive prison and a death sentence, win the presidency, and earn the Nobel Peace Prize for reaching out to the North.
In 1938 a small trading firm opened in Daegu. Samsung would grow into a giant of phones, televisions and chips.
After liberation, Chung Ju-yung founded Hyundai, a building firm that would grow into a maker of cars and ships.
Japan's rule ended in 1945, but the peninsula was split. In 1948 the Republic of Korea was founded in the south.
Two years later, North Korea invaded. The United States and its allies fought on one side, China on the other, and the war ended in a stalemate.
The armistice left a strip of land about four kilometres wide between North and South, still one of the most guarded borders on Earth.
Yoon Suk Yeol would become president, and then fall, after declaring martial law in December 2024.
From the sixties, the Miracle on the Han River began, turning one of the world's poorest countries into a rich industrial one.
Lee Jae-myung, a lawyer turned politician, would win the presidency in 2025 after Yoon's removal.
Han Kang, author of The Vegetarian, would become the first Korean to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Growth did not bring freedom. In May 1980 the people of Gwangju rose against military rule, and soldiers killed many of them.
Seven years later, millions took to the streets, and the generals gave way to direct presidential elections.
In 1988 Seoul hosted the Olympics, showing a new, democratic Korea to the world.
Kim Yuna, a young skater, would win Olympic gold at Vancouver and become a national hero.
Son Heung-min would captain the national football team and win the Premier League's Golden Boot.
In 1997 a financial crisis swept Asia, and South Korea needed a rescue loan. It recovered, and grew again.
In 2002 Korea and Japan shared the World Cup, and the South Korean team reached the semi-finals, a record for Asia.
In 2013 seven young men formed BTS. Their Korean songs would top the charts in America and win fans across the globe.
The next year brought grief: the Sewol ferry capsized, and three hundred and four people died, most of them schoolchildren.
At the Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang, athletes of North and South marched together under one flag.
Bong Joon-ho's Parasite, a dark tale of rich and poor, became the first film not in English to win the Oscar for best picture.
Then Squid Game, with its deadly children's games, became one of the most watched series Netflix had ever shown.
And in December 2024 the president declared martial law. Within hours parliament voted it down, and democracy held.
From Dangun's legend to the world's screens, South Korea has made its own remarkable story.
